source.title: Beyond Semantics: How Temporal Biases Shape Retrieval in Transformer and State-Space Models
source.authors: Anooshka Bajaj; Deven Mahesh Mistry; Sahaj Singh Maini; Y. Aggarwal; Zoran Tiganj

record.file_problem: The full paper text, including appendices and tables, is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses a different prompt and scoring setup to measure serial recall and episodic retrieval, and causally ablates heads selected by induction scores. It does not reproduce the original training-time emergence analysis.
record.gate_note: The paper reports serial-recall preferences and induction-head ablation effects relevant to V1 and V4. It also reports SSM channel ablations, recorded as findings about induction-style behavior but not as evidence that SSM channels are induction heads. No training trajectory, loss-curve bump, loss-by-token-index measure, few-shot task-learning test, or transition analysis is reported. Cited findings from prior work are not recorded as rows. Figure-only results and other reported results are omitted due to the 60-row limit; see rows_left_out.
record.test_reason: The study ablates top induction-score heads in four pretrained 7-9B instruction-tuned transformers. It measures the loss of [A][B]…[A]→[B] (+1 token) recall against matched random-head ablations. This is a new setting that bears on whether induction-behaving heads exist and matter across model families (V4). It does not study training dynamics, small attention-only models, previous-token composition, loss by token index, or few-shot task learning.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, but incomplete. The paper's main claim is that permutation-controlled probes reveal model-specific primacy/recency (lost-in-the-middle) temporal biases in serial recall and episodic retrieval, in both transformers and SSMs. Mechanistically, ablating high-induction-score heads reduces serial recall and episodic separation in transformers. In SSMs, sparse high-attribution channels play an analogous role but are not claimed to be equivalent to induction heads.
record.recipe_differences: Uses permutation-controlled random-token prompts and head/channel ablations in pretrained instruction models, rather than studying induction-head development during training. Head ranking uses an induction score; ablations zero attention scores.
record.method_sensitivity: Effects vary by model, number of repetitions and spacing in the prompt, probe position in episodic retrieval, and ablation size. The reported induction-head ablation comparison also varies by model and head count.

fits_no_version.finding: SSM and recurrent models (Mamba-130m, Falcon3-Mamba-7B, Recurrent-Gemma-9b) show a +1 serial-recall preference. Ablating 5-10% of high-attribution channels reduces the recall and episodic signals more than random channels. The authors disclaim one-to-one equivalence with induction heads.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Non-attention sequence models show induction-style copying supported by a sparse set of channels, distinct from transformer induction heads.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The experiments use random-token prompts rather than natural text, and assess next-token probabilities. Some evidence is presented only in figures. SSM channel salience is a gradient-based heuristic, and the authors state it is not a one-to-one analog of induction heads. The paper does not report per-row uncertainty for the tabulated ablation changes.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row cap was reached with the numerical ablation results in Tables A1 and A2. Omitted: the separate per-model baseline serial-recall profiles and repeat/spacing conditions in Figures 2, A1 and A3; episodic-retrieval profiles in Figure 3; transformer episodic-ablation results in Figures A4–A7; and the SSM episodic-ablation plots in Figures A8–A9. Their figure values were not transcribed into rows. Two random-head controls from Table A1 (Qwen at 1 head and Gemma at 1 head) were also omitted to retain all numerical SSM ablation conditions from Table A2.

untested.parts: Not tested. No small attention-only transformers and no analysis of composition with previous-token heads; the heads are ranked by induction score only.
Not tested. No training trajectories, abruptness or loss bump.
Not tested. No loss-by-token-index measure and no share of in-context learning attributed to induction heads.

Only one size per family (7-9B instruct) and one checkpoint each; no sweep over sizes or training runs. Induction scores themselves are not reported. No other modalities. SSM channels are explicitly not claimed to be heads.
Not tested. Training data and setup are not varied.
Not tested. No few-shot task-learning comparison.

missing.what: Random-head controls for Qwen at 1 head (8.58e-6) and Gemma at 1 head (6.56e-7)
Difference column Δ (Induction − Random) per model and ablation level, plus the summary: Δ > 0 in 13/16 settings, median 3.52e-5
Unablated +1 probability levels per transformer, needed to judge the relative size of the ~1e-5 to 2e-4 changes
Transformer episodic-retrieval ablations: induction-head ablation spreads probability across competing targets, with a weaker random effect (figures only)

record.verdict_notes: V1 links were removed from all rows because the models are 7-9B instruction-tuned transformers, not small attention-only models, and no previous-token-head composition is examined. Three reader 'reversed' states were reset to absent: the negative changes are tiny, and the authors call them small. Absolute effect sizes are small (≤2.3e-4 in probability), and no uncertainty is reported for the ablation table. Several random controls also reduce the signal noticeably. The SSM sign convention in Table A2 is unclear, and Mamba's 1% random value (−91.7%) is anomalous.

versions.untested_parts: Tests whether ablating induction-score heads affects serial recall and episodic retrieval in instruction-tuned transformers. Does not test formation by composing with an earlier previous-token head, directly analyze that composition, or use small attention-only transformers.
No training-time emergence, abruptness, loss-curve bump, or coincidence with an in-context-learning gain is measured.
Does not measure most in-context learning, token-index loss reduction, or the role of induction heads in general few-shot learning in large transformers.
Tests induction-score heads in four transformer model families. Does not sweep sizes or training runs, and SSM channels are not heads; the authors explicitly do not claim one-to-one equivalence.
Prompt repetition and spacing are varied, but training data or training setup is not varied; formation time and persistence of in-context learning are not studied.
Does not compare few-shot task learning with copying or test whether other heads or mechanisms mainly carry few-shot learning.
No training transitions or formation sub-steps are measured.

statements.correction: Table A1: weak or negative targeted differences at the specified small counts; positive targeted differences for Qwen at 50/100 heads and Gemma at 50 heads. Section 2.2: serial-recall behaviour in all tested models. These results establish variation in ablation sensitivity, without demonstrating a family lacking induction behaviour.
statements.problem: The numerical summary is correct, but treating weak small-count ablation effects as limits_scope on V4 conflates concentration or causal specificity with the existence of induction behaviour across families.
